interactive.title: Tiles into a rectangle
interactive.whatAmILookingAt: A short lesson in thirteen small screens on the tiles from lesson 1, now handed to you loose. An x² tile is an x by x square, an x-strip is x long and 1 wide, and a unit square is 1 by 1. A quadratic such as x² + 5x + 6 is one x² tile, 5 strips and 6 unit squares. They glide into one rectangle, and on one screen you drag knobs to change how many strips go along each side. The x² tile sits in the top-left corner, the strips lie along its right side and its bottom edge, and the unit squares fill the bottom-right corner between them. If a strips go one way and b the other, that corner is a by b, so it needs a × b squares. The rectangle closes only when the squares fill that corner exactly and every strip is used, and then its width and height read off as the two brackets, x + a and x + b. A wrong split leaves a gap or an overhang, and a count beside it shows the strips and squares that rectangle would need against the ones you have. For 2x², two x² tiles sit side by side, so that side is 2x long. Where a quadratic has a minus sign, the tiles become lesson 1's grid filled in backwards: x² goes in the top-left cell, the number on its own in the bottom-right cell, and the two other cells must add up to the x term. A cell below zero is hatched, because no tile can have an area below zero. Some screens show an idea and the rest ask you to try it. A puzzle offers three answers. A wrong pick shows its own rectangle or grid, with what it would need, or is checked by putting a number into the quadratic and into that answer, which come out different.
interactive.ignores: The tiles draw x as one positive length, and they are to scale only for the x drawn. x can be any number, negative or a fraction, and every factorising here still holds. The grid's hatched cells are terms below zero, not areas. Only whole-number pairs are tried, so the quadratics are chosen to have one. A quadratic with no whole-number pair, such as x² + 4x + 1, may still split into brackets with other numbers, and later lessons find them.

explain.text:
Factorising is expanding run backwards. In lesson 1 you had the two brackets and found the tiles. Now you are handed the tiles and must find the rectangle, because its two sides are the brackets. x² + 5x + 6 is one x² tile, 5 strips and 6 unit squares. Put the x² tile in a corner and the strips along its two sides, say a of them along one side and b along the other. That leaves an a by b corner to fill with unit squares, so the rectangle closes only when the strips split into a pair that adds to 5 and the same pair multiplies to 6. This is lesson 1's (x + a)(x + b) = x² + (a + b)x + ab read from the right: to factorise x² + bx + c, the two numbers in the brackets must add to b and multiply to c.[^1] Of the whole-number pairs that make 6, 1 and 6 add to 7, and only 2 and 3 add to 5, so x² + 5x + 6 = (x + 2)(x + 3). The brackets and the tiles are two ways of writing the same area, so they are equal,[^2] and trying a number usually catches a slip: at x = 4, (x + 2)(x + 3) is 6 × 7 = 42, and 16 + 20 + 6 = 42. An easy slip is (x + 3)(x + 3), since 3 + 3 is 6 too, but that rectangle needs 9 squares and 6 strips, which is x² + 6x + 9.

A minus sign has no tile, so lesson 1's grid takes over, filled in backwards: x² in one corner, the number on its own in the opposite corner, and the two other cells must add to the x term. For x² − x − 12 the pair must multiply to −12 and add to −1. Only opposite signs multiply to a minus, as in Negative numbers, so one number is positive and one negative, and their sum is as big as the gap between their sizes. 4 and 3 have a gap of 1, and the sum is −1, so the 4 takes the minus: x² − x − 12 = (x − 4)(x + 3). When the number on its own is positive and the x term negative, both numbers are negative. A pair also works with no x term at all, as long as it adds to 0. For x² − 49 that is 7 and −7, whose strips cancel, as in lesson 1's (x + 3)(x − 3), so x² − 49 = (x + 7)(x − 7), a [[difference of two squares]]. With a pair of equal numbers the rectangle is a square, so x² − 6x + 9 = (x − 3)², a [[perfect square]].

Before looking for a pair, take out any common factor, as in Linear equations, so the brackets are smaller. x² + 2x has no unit squares, so it is x(x + 2), and 2x² + 10x + 12 = 2(x² + 5x + 6) = 2(x + 2)(x + 3). When x² has a number in front that will not come out, as in 2x² + 7x + 3, the pair must multiply to 2 × 3 = 6 and add to 7. The reason is in the rectangle whose sides are 2x + 1 and 1x + 3. Its 2 x² tiles are 2 × 1, and its 3 squares are 1 × 3. Its strips come in two blocks, 2 × 3 = 6 one way and 1 × 1 = 1 the other, and the two blocks use the same four numbers once each, so 6 × 1 is the same as 2 × 3. So split 7x into 6x + x and group the four terms in twos: 2x² + 6x = 2x(x + 3) and x + 3 = 1(x + 3). Both groups hold (x + 3), so it comes out as a common factor, leaving (2x + 1)(x + 3). Some quadratics, such as x² + 4x + 1, have no whole-number pair, because only 1 and 1, or −1 and −1, multiply to 1, and neither adds to 4. Later lessons find other numbers for many of those, and show why some have none.

Brackets are worth finding because a product can be read at a glance, and lesson 3 uses them to find where a quadratic is zero. **To factorise x² + bx + c, find two numbers that add to b and multiply to c,[^1] so x² + 5x + 6 = (x + 2)(x + 3), and check by expanding back.**

analogy.text: Say a rectangular deck hatch takes 10 m of seal round its edge and has an opening of 6 m². Half the seal, 5 m, is one long side plus one short side, and the two sides multiply to 6 m². 2 m and 3 m is the pair that does both, so the hatch is 2 m by 3 m, just as 2 and 3 split x² + 5x + 6.
analogy.breaks: A hatch's sides are positive lengths, so it cannot show a pair with a minus sign, such as −4 and 3 for x² − x − 12, which needs the grid. Its two numbers are the sides themselves, while each bracket adds its number to x, and x can be any number.

practice.text:
- Take out any common factor first.
- For x² + bx + c, list pairs that multiply to c and pick the one that adds to b.[^1]
- With a number a in front of x² that will not come out, find a pair that multiplies to a × c and adds to b, split the x term with it and group in twos.
- Write the brackets.
- Expand them back, or try a number in the quadratic and in your brackets, then a second number.

**Rule of thumb:** If c is positive, both numbers take the sign of b. If c is negative, one is plus and one minus, and the one bigger in size takes the sign of b. No x term means the pair adds to 0.

**Worked example:** 2x² + 2x − 12. Every term divides by 2, so it is 2(x² + x − 6). The pair must multiply to −6 and add to 1, so one is negative, and 3 and −2 work. That gives 2(x + 3)(x − 2). As a check, at x = 3 the quadratic makes 18 + 6 − 12 = 12, and the brackets make 2 × 6 × 1 = 12.

**Common mistakes**
- A pair that adds right but multiplies wrong, so x² + 5x + 6 becomes (x + 3)(x + 3). That is x² + 6x + 9.
- Swapping the signs, so x² + 2x − 15 becomes (x − 5)(x + 3). That adds to −2, not 2. Try x = 4, which gives −7 against 9.
- Missing the common factor, so x² + 6x is forced into two brackets. It is x(x + 6).
- With a number in front, using a pair that multiplies to c alone, so 3x² + 10x + 8 becomes (3x + 2)(x + 4). The pair must multiply to 3 × 8 = 24, which gives 6 and 4, and (3x + 4)(x + 2).

interactive.html:
The loose tiles of a quadratic put together into one rectangle, then lesson 1's grid filled in backwards for a minus sign. The quadratics are examples chosen to factorise with whole numbers.

A rectangle's two sides are the brackets, and its tiles added up are the quadratic.
interactive.title: Tiles into a rectangle
interactive.brief: The one thing you should see is the tiles of x² + 5x + 6 closing into a rectangle only when the 6 squares split 2 by 3 to match the strips, when you watch them glide into place or drag the knobs on step 3 to try other splits.

checks.label: To factorise x² + bx + c, the sum of the two numbers in the brackets must be b and the product must be c: on every screen the answer's two numbers do both (after any common factor), and the answer equals its quadratic at every number tried, whole, a half or negative

The brackets and the tiles are two ways of expressing the same area, so they are equal: every rectangle a screen closes is exactly as wide times as tall as all its tiles together, one tile for each term of the quadratic

The rectangle of x² + 5x + 6 closes only for 2 and 3 strips (either way round): for every split from 0 to 6 strips on each side it needs that many strips added and squares multiplied, and any other split leaves tiles missing or left over
(x + 3)(x + 3) needs 9 squares and 6 strips, which is x² + 6x + 9: built from the 6 squares and 5 strips of x² + 5x + 6 it has 3 squares and 1 strip missing
Pairs making 6: 1 and 6 add to 7, and 2 and 3 add to 5; of the pairs making 8, only 2 and 4 add to 6, and of those making 20, only 4 and 5 add to 9

Every count and value listed is right: (x + 3)(x + 3) needs 9 squares, (x + 1)(x + 8) 9 strips, (x + 2)(x + 10) 12 strips, (x + 3)(x + 6) 18 squares, (3x + 2)(x + 4) 14 strips and (3x + 8)(x + 1) 11; the values at x = 5, 4, 1 and 3 match by hand; and every line of working adds up

Each puzzle accepts only its right answer, and every wrong answer offered is a different quadratic: its rectangle is left with tiles missing or left over, its grid has a cell that does not match, or it makes a different value at the number tried

Before an answer, a puzzle's picture gives nothing away: its tiles lie loose, or its grid shows only the x² term and the number on its own (2x² and −8, nothing taken out, for 2x² − 8), with ? on the unknown sides
A cell is hatched exactly when its term is below zero: −4x and −12 in x² − x − 12, while in (x − 3)² the corner −3 × −3 makes 9 and is not
Every demonstration has finished arriving within 4.5 s of its screen opening, none starting before the 0.35 s screen fade ends; every answer's motion, right or wrong, within 2 s

applied.problem: Three overstatements: one number does not always catch a slip (x = 0 gives 6 for both x² + 5x + 6 and (x + 1)(x + 6)); a sum like 3 + (−4) is −1, only as big as the gap; and quadratics with no whole-number pair such as x² + x + 1 have no real numbers to find (i5: "that has them").
"The bigger one takes the sign of b" is ambiguous on a review card: after signing, 3 is bigger than −4 in x² − x − 12, yet −4 is the one with b's sign; the rule means the one bigger in size.
